title: Teaching on Purpose #7: Whole Class Feedback
author: Adam Kohlbeck
summary: This is the seventh installment in Adam Kohlbeck's 'Teaching on Purpose' series, documenting conversations with teachers at Chiltern Learning Trust about specific instructional techniques aligned to six core teaching purposes. This week's purpose is 'Communicate Meaning' and the technique is Whole Class Feedback -- providing collective feedback to a class following a piece of work, highlighting excellent effort, naming common misconceptions, and creating an immediate opportunity to apply the feedback. Kohlbeck interviews Lauren Pickering, Assistant Headteacher and MFL teacher, who explains three usage scenarios: the standard case (developing skills across a unit, where multiple students show different mastery levels benefiting from collective address); an adapted case (using the feedback window to pre-teach a skill needed in a future unit rather than correcting current work); and a case where the technique is not the right tool (Key Stage 4 exam preparation, where modeling exam technique through 'walking talking mocks' is more appropriate). The article distinguishes whole class feedback from traditional written comments in individual books, arguing the latter is less effective because it depends on students independently extracting meaning from written text and sustaining engagement with it.
points: Whole class feedback provides collective rather than individual commentary, centering on examples of excellent work, common misconceptions, and re-teaching with immediate application -- making the feedback loop visible to the whole room rather than siloed in individual books.

The technique is more effective than written book comments because individual written feedback requires students to independently extract meaning, while whole class feedback allows the teacher to explain, re-teach, and have students apply it immediately.

The 'look ahead' adaptation -- using the feedback window to pre-teach a skill needed in a future unit -- capitalizes on time already set aside to accelerate future learning without waiting for the skill to appear on the next assignment.

Whole class feedback is the wrong tool for Key Stage 4 exam preparation, where content is typically secure and the barrier is exam technique -- walking talking mocks are more appropriate in that context.

The technique exemplifies deliberate technique selection: knowing which of the six core teaching purposes (securing attention, communicating meaning, driving thinking, enabling practice, utilizing memory, checking for understanding) a lesson moment is serving.
quotes: Whole class feedback is a technique for providing collective feedback to a class following a piece of work. It typically involves the teacher identifying examples of excellent work or efforts, common misconceptions and errors and then feeding this back to a whole class. They then provide the opportunity to apply the feedback they have received.

This technique is different from traditional approaches to feedback which usually include written comments in individual pupil books. This style of written feedback can be less effective as it relies on students drawing the intended meaning from what the teacher has written.

In an English unit, the teacher might have introduced the use of Fronted Adverbials and be revisiting subordinating conjunctions. They will then re-teach it and provide an activity that enables the students to apply this feedback immediately.

Whole class feedback needs to be adapted when there is an opportunity to focus on something that will be especially important in future units of work. This adaptation is useful because it capitalises on the time that the teacher has set aside for feedback to move learning on.
In Key stage 4, during exam preparation, the teacher may be better served by running a walking, talking exam where they model how to answer questions and students engage as part of that process.
